2. Number Systems

From naturals to reals — building the number systems from axioms, and telling countable infinities from uncountable ones.

  • Natural Numbers and Induction — The natural numbers start from the Peano axioms: P(1)P(1)P(1) plus P(k)⇒P(k+1)P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1)P(k)⇒P(k+1) yields P(n)P(n)P(n) for every natural number nnn — addition and multiplication are also defined recursively, and this one principle proves infinitely many statements at once.
  • The Binomial Theorem — The binomial theorem (x+y)n=∑k=0n(nk)xn−kyk(x+y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^{n-k}y^k(x+y)n=∑k=0n​(kn​)xn−kyk proved by induction — Pascal's identity (nk)+(nk−1)=(n+1k)\binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}=\binom{n+1}{k}(kn​)+(k−1n​)=(kn+1​) is the inductive step, and row nnn of Pascal's triangle is drawn live.
  • Integers and Rationals — Integers arise as equivalence classes of natural pairs with (a,b)∼(c,d)  ⟺  a+d=b+c(a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c(a,b)∼(c,d)⟺a+d=b+c, and rationals as classes of integer pairs with (a,b)∼(c,d)  ⟺  ad=bc(a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff ad=bc(a,b)∼(c,d)⟺ad=bc. The "numbers as equivalence classes" trick returns when the reals are built from the rationals.
  • √2 is Irrational — Plotting the rationals p/qp/qp/q with denominator at most NNN on [1,2][1, 2][1,2] leaves a hole at 2≈1.4142\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41422​≈1.4142 — no NNN ever fills it. Proposition 4.4.4: no rational squares to 222.
  • Density of the Rationals — Every open interval (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) contains a rational: with n=⌊1/(y−x)⌋+1n = \lfloor 1/(y-x) \rfloor + 1n=⌊1/(y−x)⌋+1 and m=⌊nx⌋+1m = \lfloor nx \rfloor + 1m=⌊nx⌋+1, x<m/n<yx < m/n < yx<m/n<y. Watch the rational ticks inside the interval multiply as the denominator cap grows.
  • Sets and Functions — See set operations A∪BA \cup BA∪B, A∩BA \cap BA∩B, AcA^cAc, De Morgan's laws, and injective / surjective / bijective maps as pictures.
  • The Axiom of Choice — A function picking one element from each set in a collection — for finite collections no axiom is needed, but for infinite ones this "picking" is itself an axiom. Pick one dot per row.
  • Zorn's Lemma — If every chain has an upper bound, a maximal element exists — light up the chains one by one in the divisibility poset of 12's divisors. Equivalent to the axiom of choice, the master key of algebra.
  • The Supremum Axiom — Every bounded-above set has a least upper bound sup⁡S\sup SsupS — the axiom filling the gaps in the rationals, twin of the rational-holes scene.
  • Existence of n-th Roots — The supremum of {x≥0:xn<a}\{x \ge 0 : x^n < a\}{x≥0:xn<a} IS an\sqrt[n]{a}na​ — watch the supremum axiom fill a "gap" and manufacture a root.
  • Countable vs Uncountable — The rationals fit into a single list; the reals do not — verified by Cantor's diagonal argument.
  • Cantor's Theorem — Every set is smaller than its power set — ∣X∣<∣P(X)∣|X| < |\mathcal{P}(X)|∣X∣<∣P(X)∣. The diagonal-flipped set differs from every row of the list. (This is the theorem itself, not the Cantor "set" scene.)
  • Groups vs Fields — A group is reversible moves (associativity, identity, inverses); a field is a world where all four operations work. Includes the subgroup test and (Z,+)(\mathbb{Z},+)(Z,+) vs (Q,+,×)(\mathbb{Q},+,\times)(Q,+,×).
  • Vector Spaces and Isomorphism — A vector space is an abelian group over a field with scalar multiplication — Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn, sequence spaces, and spaces of continuous functions are the same structure in different packaging. Move (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) and the line y=a+bxy = a+bxy=a+bx and the point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) move together.
  • Dimension and Rank — If isomorphism means "same structure", dimension and rank measure its size. Watch the grid get squeezed by a matrix and verify dim⁡ker⁡T+rank T=dim⁡V\dim\ker T + \mathrm{rank}\,T = \dim VdimkerT+rankT=dimV.
